title: QuCLEAR: Clifford Extraction and Absorption for Quantum Circuit Optimization
problem: Near-term quantum devices have high gate error rates, and the dominant approach of reducing two-qubit gate count via peephole optimization or routing-aware compilation leaves substantial overhead from Clifford subcircuits that could be eliminated rather than merely rearranged.
method: QuCLEAR is a compilation framework with two sequential optimization steps. First, Clifford Extraction identifies and extracts Clifford subcircuits from the original circuit, commuting them to the end of the circuit via a series of gate commutation rules while simultaneously optimizing (reducing) the remaining non-Clifford gates; this process changes the structure of the remaining circuit to expose further simplifications. Second, Clifford Absorption leverages the classical simulatability of Clifford circuits to compute their effect analytically and absorb (classically post-process) the extracted Clifford subcircuit rather than executing it on quantum hardware, eliminating those gates entirely from the quantum circuit.

title: SparseWeaver: Converting Sparse Operations as Dense Operations on GPUs for Graph Workloads
problem: Real-world graph workloads have sparse and skewed adjacency structures that cause severe warp-level load imbalance on GPUs, where existing software or hardware balancing schemes incur memory overhead or excessive inter- and intra-warp synchronization cost.
method: SparseWeaver is a hardware-software co-design that converts sparse graph operations into balanced dense operations by exploiting graph topology. A lightweight GPU functional unit microarchitecture called Weaver is added to GPU cores; it analyzes common sparse-to-dense conversion patterns identified via static/dynamic analysis and implements the conversion directly in the execution pipeline, leveraging memory access locality without additional synchronization. The design is prototyped on the open-source RISC-V Vortex GPU.

title: Exo 2: Growing a Scheduling Language
problem: User-schedulable languages (USLs) fix a single design point for what programmers control and what is automated, but no universal control/automation split exists even in narrow domains, causing USLs to be inextensible when new hardware targets or optimization strategies emerge.
method: Exo 2 enables users to define new scheduling operations externally to the compiler by composing a set of trusted fine-grained primitives (actions for modifying code, inspection for querying code structure, and references for pointing to code locations). The key mechanism is Cursors, a new abstraction that unifies code references across actions, inspections, and scheduling library composition, allowing safe user-defined scheduling transformations. Users build scheduling libraries that amortize transformation effort across related kernels without modifying the compiler internals.

title: SYLQ-SV: Scaling Symbolic Execution of Hardware Designs with Query Caching
problem: Symbolic execution of hardware designs (in SystemVerilog) suffers from path explosion, making full security and functional verification intractably expensive. Existing engines lack comprehensive SystemVerilog language support and do not exploit redundancy across SMT queries generated during path exploration.
method: SylQ-SV is a dedicated SystemVerilog symbolic execution engine that caches SMT queries across paths. When the engine encounters a query that is semantically equivalent to a previously solved one, it retrieves the cached result rather than re-invoking the SMT solver, avoiding redundant computation. The engine also provides full SystemVerilog language coverage including SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) to support end-to-end verification of open-source designs.

title: KernelGPT: Enhanced Kernel Fuzzing via Large Language Models
problem: Kernel fuzzing effectiveness depends critically on syscall specifications that define the syntax and semantics of system calls, but generating these specifications is largely manual work, leaving large numbers of important syscalls uncovered and limiting automated kernel vulnerability discovery.
method: KernelGPT uses large language models to automatically generate and repair syscall specifications for kernel fuzzing. The system prompts an LLM with kernel source code and documentation to synthesize syscall specifications in the format expected by the Syzkaller fuzzer, then uses an iterative refinement loop where fuzzing feedback is fed back to the LLM to repair invalid or incomplete specifications. This LLM-guided specification generation covers previously uncovered syscalls and improves the semantic validity of generated syscall sequences.

title: Accelerating Simulation of Quantum Circuits under Noise via Computational Reuse
problem: Noisy quantum circuit simulation on HPC systems is prohibitively slow because simulators must iteratively re-execute nearly identical circuits thousands of times across different noise model trials, recomputing the same intermediate quantum states from scratch each time.
method: TQSim (Tree-Based Quantum Circuit Simulation) dynamically partitions a quantum circuit into subcircuits and constructs a tree of intermediate results that can be reused across different noisy simulation trials. The system identifies which subcircuit branches diverge due to noise injection and reuses cached intermediate density matrix or statevector results for the converging branches, avoiding redundant re-simulation. The approach is designed for multi-node distributed HPC setups with tight fidelity bounds on the approximation.

title: AsyncDIMM: Achieving Asynchronous Execution in DIMM-Based Near-Memory Processing
problem: DIMM-based near-memory processing (NMP) architectures cannot efficiently support asynchronous execution between host CPUs and near-memory accelerators (NMAs) because independent memory controllers on both sides cause memory bus contention and potential DRAM errors when issuing concurrent accesses. Existing designs resort to synchronous execution, wasting either host or NMA compute.
method: AsyncDIMM introduces three operational modes on existing memory buses: single access (host or NMA only), concurrent access, and seamless mode switching. An offload-schedule-return mechanism with explicit and implicit synchronization ensures correct memory access semantics across modes. Optimized timing constraints reduce offload latency; a locality-aware switch-recovery method minimizes mode-switch overhead; adaptive batching with timing-division multiplexing notifications improves return bandwidth. Hardware modifications are limited to conventional host and NMA memory controllers and validated on FPGA.

title: LIA: A Single-GPU LLM Inference Acceleration with Cooperative AMX-Enabled CPU-GPU Computation and CXL Offloading
problem: Single-GPU LLM inference is constrained by GPU memory capacity, forcing either expensive multi-GPU deployments or frequent CPU-GPU transfers over slow PCIe, which bottleneck both latency and throughput.
method: LIA is a single-GPU LLM inference framework that systematically offloads matrix computations to AMX-enabled CPUs (4th-gen Sapphire Rapids and 6th-gen Granite Rapids Xeon), reducing CPU-GPU transfers by keeping model parameters near the CPU. LIA introduces a memory-offloading policy that integrates CXL memory (as an affordable DRAM extension) with DDR memory to expand effective model capacity for throughput-oriented batch workloads. The system partitions transformer layer computations between CPU and GPU based on runtime latency/throughput objectives, using AMX tile instructions for high-throughput GEMM on the CPU side.

title: Fusion: An Analytics Object Store Optimized for Query Pushdown
problem: Disaggregated cloud storage uses erasure coding that partitions analytics file objects into fixed-size blocks across storage nodes; when query predicates are pushed down to storage (computation pushdown), the storage system must reassemble objects across nodes, incurring high network latency that undermines pushdown's intended benefits for ad-hoc and highly-selective OLAP queries.
method: Fusion is an analytics object store that co-designs storage layout and query pushdown execution for erasure-coded environments. It reorganizes how analytics file objects (e.g., Parquet files) are partitioned and distributed across storage nodes so that query-relevant data stripes can be accessed and evaluated locally at storage nodes without full object reassembly. Pushdown execution is coordinated across storage nodes in a way that respects erasure coding boundaries, enabling predicate evaluation close to data while minimizing cross-node communication.

title: Tela: A Temporal Load-Aware Cloud Virtual Disk Placement Scheme
problem: Cloud Virtual Disk (CVD) placement algorithms for Cloud Block Storage do not account for temporal load fluctuations, leading to imbalanced storage warehouse loads, low resource utilization, and frequent overloads under dynamic workloads.
method: Tela introduces a temporal load-aware CVD placement scheme that models and predicts time-varying I/O load patterns for each physical storage warehouse, then uses these temporal load predictions to make placement decisions that balance load both at placement time and over future intervals, avoiding placements that would create future overloads.

title: Gemina: A Coordinated and High-Performance Memory Deduplication Engine
problem: Memory deduplication (via KSM) eliminates duplicate pages but forces huge pages to split into 4KB base pages, degrading TLB hit rates and memory access performance by up to 43%; asynchronous huge page promotion cannot recover this loss because deduplication breaks the uniformity of page attributes required for promotion.
method: Gemina coordinates huge page management with memory deduplication through three components: (1) a fine-grained detector that separately classifies pages by both redundancy and access hotness to decouple deduplication decisions from page-size decisions; (2) a distributor that conservatively processes pages to avoid frequent hot/cold and size-class switches; and (3) an adapter that reorganizes memory layout to enable fast base-to-huge-page conversion. Together, these components preserve huge page availability by selectively deferring or avoiding deduplication of hot pages while still capturing most memory savings.

title: Necro-reaper: Pruning away Dead Memory Traffic in Warehouse-Scale Computers
problem: A significant fraction of memory traffic in warehouse-scale computers (WSC) is unnecessary: it consists of writebacks of deallocated (dead) heap data and fetches of uninitialized data, neither of which carries useful information. Short-lived heap allocations larger than a cache line—common in WSC—exacerbate this problem.
method: Necro-reaper is a software/hardware co-design that introduces new ISA instructions to let the hardware skip unnecessary dead memory traffic without requiring hardware-level tracking of live/dead data. A profile-guided compiler analyzes allocation lifetimes and annotates call sites with the new instructions. A customized memory allocator extends these annotations to inform the hardware at deallocation time. The approach leverages WSC's existing vertical integration (shared hardware, OS, compiler, and allocator stack) to make the analysis and insertion of instructions practical.

title: FlexSP: Accelerating Large Language Model Training via Flexible Sequence Parallelism
problem: Existing sequence parallelism methods for long-context LLM training assume homogeneous (equal-length) sequences and apply a single static scattering strategy, causing severe load imbalance when real training corpora have heterogeneous, long-tail sequence length distributions.
method: FlexSP introduces flexible sequence parallelism that adapts the scattering strategy per-sequence to match each sequence's actual length. The system dynamically selects the degree of sequence parallelism and the scattering pattern (e.g., how many devices a sequence is split across) based on the length distribution of the current batch, balancing workload across devices and reducing idle time from length imbalance. Communication and attention computation are co-optimized under the flexible strategy.

title: Tackling ML-based Dynamic Mispredictions using Statically Computed Invariants for Attack Surface Reduction
problem: ML-based runtime predictors used for code debloating and dynamic control flow monitoring lack guarantees that distinguish mispredictions from actual security attacks, making them unsuitable for safety-critical security contexts. Without this distinction, the system either blocks legitimate executions (false positives from mispredictions) or fails to stop real attacks.
method: The paper computes static program invariants at compile/analysis time to reduce the attack surface that ML-based dynamic predictors must cover. Statically proven safe behaviors are removed from the ML decision space, so the ML model only makes predictions over a reduced, ambiguous region. When the ML predictor fires on the reduced set, the probability that it is a misprediction versus an actual attack is much lower, enabling more reliable enforcement in security settings such as control flow integrity and debloating.

title: REACT3D: Real-time Edge Accelerator for Incremental Training in 3D Gaussian Splatting based SLAM Systems
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM requires incremental training and rendering at over 30 FPS on edge devices, but existing GPU-based solutions and prior accelerators fall short due to redundant training computation, unnecessary loss computation, and irregular memory access patterns. The combination of continuous camera streaming, per-Gaussian gradient accumulation, and sparse activated Gaussian sets creates severe compute and memory irregularity.
method: REACT3D introduces two algorithmic optimizations: (1) spatial consistency and convergence-aware sparsification that predicts under-optimized Gaussians based on spatial coherence and convergence dynamics, eliminating redundant forward/backward rendering passes; and (2) a pixel block-wise fine-grained dataflow that fuses loss computation into the rendering pipeline, removing explicit loss storage. At the architectural level, a Content Addressable Memory (CAM)-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer resolves discontinuous memory accesses by maintaining two parallel indices into the Gaussian buffer, avoiding computation conflicts during gradient merging across scattered Gaussian-to-pixel mappings.

title: DAPPER: A Performance-Attack-Resilient Tracker for RowHammer Defense
problem: Host-side RowHammer mitigation mechanisms rely on shared counter or tracking structures that are vulnerable to Performance Attacks (Perf-Attacks), where adversaries reverse-engineer the shared structure's mapping to artificially inflate DRAM access counters or trigger early resets, degrading performance of co-running benign applications.
method: DAPPER introduces secure hashing to randomize the mapping of DRAM rows to shared tracking structures, preventing adversaries from predicting counter locations. DAPPER-S provides a base secure hashing template using a single hash function. DAPPER-H extends this with double-hashing, novel reset strategies that avoid predictable early resets, and mitigative refresh techniques that piggyback RowHammer mitigations onto scheduled refresh operations to amortize overhead. The combined design uses only 96KB of SRAM per 32GB of DRAM, validated against 57 workloads from SPEC2006, SPEC2017, TPC, Hadoop, MediaBench, and YCSB.
